name: Universals and substances ('this' versus 'such')
plain_explanation: A proper name like 'Napoleon' picks out one particular, unrepeatable thing; a word like 'man' or 'white' can apply to many different things. Aristotle calls what a proper name signifies a 'substance,' and what a general word signifies a 'universal.'
precise_definition: Aristotle's definition: 'By the term universal I mean that which is of such a nature as to be predicated of many subjects, by individual that which is not thus predicated.' A substance is a 'this'; a universal is a 'such,' indicating a sort of thing rather than a particular thing, and (Aristotle holds) cannot itself be a substance, since substance is 'peculiar' to one thing while a universal is common to many.
why_it_mattered: It is Aristotle's proposed replacement for Plato's Ideas: what is common to many red things ('redness') depends for its being on there being red things, but not vice versa -- yet, as Russell shows, this common-sense-seeming asymmetry does not survive careful analysis.
historical_origin: Set out in Aristotle's On Interpretation and Categories.
examples: Football (a universal-like activity) could not exist without football-players, though it could exist without this or that particular player
Redness cannot exist without some subject, but can exist without this or that particular subject
objections: Russell argues the supposed asymmetry is illusory: just as a quality cannot exist without some subject, a subject cannot exist without some quality either -- so the 'true ground of the distinction is, in fact, linguistic; it is derived from syntax,' not metaphysics
competing_positions: Plato's theory that universals (Ideas) are themselves substantial, independently existing things
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly generated the medieval dispute between nominalists (who deny universals any extra-linguistic reality) and realists (who affirm it), since Aristotle's own position was left unclear.
